subtopic_detail: PJP and toxoplasma prophylaxis CD4 thresholds
stem:
A 41-year-old man with newly diagnosed HIV infection is reviewed in the immunology clinic. He has had untreated HIV for an unknown duration and presented with a 4 week history of dry cough and exertional dyspnoea, with desaturation from 96 percent to 88 percent on a 6 minute walk test. He has had thrush and seborrhoeic dermatitis. His CD4 count is 134 cells/microL, HIV viral load 480 000 copies/mL, and toxoplasma IgG positive.

CMV IgG positive, CMV IgM negative. Latent TB has been excluded with QuantiFERON-TB Gold. He has no prior allergic reactions to sulfonamides. CXR shows bilateral perihilar interstitial infiltrates. Sputum induction PCR detects Pneumocystis jirovecii. Treatment for the active PJP infection is to be commenced and the team is planning ongoing chemoprophylaxis. He is to start antiretroviral therapy within two weeks. He has no haematological cytopenias, normal LFTs and a creatinine of 78 micromol/L.

data_table.Vital signs: T 37.6, HR 96, RR 22, SpO2 92 percent room air, desat to 88 percent on exertion.
data_table.Examination: Oral candidiasis, seborrhoeic dermatitis, fine crackles bilaterally.
data_table.Investigations: CD4 134, viral load 480 000, Toxo IgG +, CMV IgG +, IgM -, QFT negative, sputum PCR PJP positive, CXR perihilar infiltrates.

lead_in: Which long-term opportunistic infection prophylaxis is most appropriate at his current CD4 count?

options.text: Azithromycin 1250 mg weekly for Mycobacterium avium complex prophylaxis only
options.rationale: MAC prophylaxis is indicated at CD4 <50 cells/microL, which he is well above (134). His most urgent prophylaxis need is PJP cover (threshold <200). Azithromycin alone misses PJP and toxoplasma. MAC prophylaxis is correct at CD4 <50 in addition to PJP/toxo cover (ASHM HIV Management Guidelines).

options.text: Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole 160/800 mg daily covering PJP and toxoplasma
options.rationale: PJP primary prophylaxis is indicated at CD4 < 200 cells/microL; toxoplasma prophylaxis is added when CD4 < 100 cells/microL AND toxoplasma IgG positive. TMP-SMX 160/800 mg daily covers both - and at this CD4 (134) he meets PJP threshold and will need toxo cover if he drops further (ASHM HIV Management Guidelines).

options.text: Valganciclovir 900 mg daily for CMV prophylaxis
options.rationale: Routine CMV primary prophylaxis is not recommended; CMV monitoring with pre-emptive therapy is reserved for CD4 <50 with detectable CMV viraemia. The anti-pattern is treating every opportunistic infection prophylactically rather than risk-stratifying. CMV-directed therapy is correct for proven CMV disease or pre-emptive in CD4 <50 with viraemia (ASHM HIV Management Guidelines).

options.text: Itraconazole 200 mg daily for endemic fungal prophylaxis
options.rationale: Endemic fungal prophylaxis is geography-specific (Histoplasma in endemic regions, Talaromyces in SE Asia); it is not routine in Australia and does not address the PJP risk. Itraconazole is correct only in geographically endemic exposures with advanced HIV (ASHM HIV Management Guidelines).

options.text: Isoniazid 300 mg daily for latent TB prophylaxis
options.rationale: Latent TB has been excluded by QuantiFERON-TB Gold; isoniazid prophylaxis is reserved for confirmed latent TB infection (positive QFT-Gold or TST). The anti-pattern is treating without confirmed indication. Isoniazid + B6 is correct only with confirmed latent TB and no active TB (ASHM HIV Management Guidelines).

explanation.summary: Opportunistic infection prophylaxis in HIV is CD4-driven: PJP < 200, toxoplasma < 100 if IgG positive, MAC < 50. TMP-SMX covers both PJP and toxoplasma. Stop prophylaxis when CD4 sustains > 200 for at least 3 months on antiretroviral therapy (ASHM).
key_points: Stop prophylaxis when CD4 > 200 sustained 3 months on cART
explanation.pearls: TMP-SMX dual-covers PJP and toxoplasma - the most efficient single agent.

subtopic_detail: Submassive PE - risk stratification and escalation
stem:
A 71-year-old man with metastatic prostate cancer is admitted with 36 hours of progressive dyspnoea. CTPA confirms a large saddle pulmonary embolism. He is alert, blood pressure 122/74 mmHg, heart rate 108 sinus, SpO2 93% on 4 L nasal prongs. Echocardiogram shows moderate right ventricular dilatation with hypokinesis of the free wall and preserved apical contractility, tricuspid annular plane systolic excursion (TAPSE) 14 mm.

High-sensitivity troponin 92 ng/L (reference <14), N-terminal pro-brain natriuretic peptide (NT-proBNP) 1850 pg/mL. Lactate 1.8 mmol/L. The simplified Pulmonary Embolism Severity Index (sPESI) is 3. He is on no anticoagulant; last fall was 3 weeks ago without head strike.

data_table.Echo: Moderate RV dilatation, free-wall hypokinesis, TAPSE 14 mm, McConnell sign present.
data_table.Imaging: CTPA: saddle PE with bilateral lobar extension.
data_table.Bloods: hs-troponin 92 ng/L (<14), NT-proBNP 1850 pg/mL, lactate 1.8 mmol/L, INR 1.1.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.text: Therapeutic enoxaparin with monitored bed for haemodynamic deterioration
options.rationale: ESC intermediate-high risk PE (RV dysfunction plus biomarker elevation without shock) is managed with therapeutic anticoagulation in a monitored setting, with rescue thrombolysis reserved for haemodynamic decompensation. Routine thrombolysis in this group does not improve mortality and significantly increases major bleeding (PEITHO trial).

options.text: Systemic alteplase 100 mg over 2 hours plus unfractionated heparin
options.rationale: Routine systemic thrombolysis in normotensive intermediate-risk PE doubles the rate of major bleeding (including intracranial haemorrhage) without a mortality benefit. Reserved for decompensation (PEITHO; ESC).

options.text: Apixaban 10 mg twice daily for 7 days then 5 mg twice daily without monitoring
options.rationale: DOACs are acceptable for low-risk PE but the intermediate-high tier warrants parenteral anticoagulation initially with monitored bed for early decompensation. Cancer-associated VTE additionally favours LMWH or apixaban with cancer-specific evidence (eTG).

Catheter-directed lysis is an emerging option in select intermediate-high risk patients but is not first-line in Australian practice and is limited to centres with interventional radiology expertise. Therapeutic anticoagulation with monitoring is the standard initial step (ESC/RACP).

options.text: Inferior vena caval filter and start warfarin with bridging heparin
options.rationale: IVC filter is reserved for absolute anticoagulation contraindication. Warfarin bridging is obsolete for acute VTE because of inferior outcomes versus LMWH/DOAC during initial therapy (eTG).

explanation.summary: PE is stratified into four tiers: high-risk (shock - thrombolyse), intermediate-high (RV dysfunction + biomarker rise, normotensive - anticoagulate + monitor), intermediate-low (one of RV/biomarker - anticoagulate), low (neither - consider outpatient). Routine lysis of intermediate-high PE worsens outcomes through bleeding.
key_points: PEITHO: routine lysis in intermediate-high PE = same mortality, more bleeding
Rescue lysis triggers: sustained hypotension, rising lactate, worsening RV
McConnell sign (apical sparing) is specific but insensitive for acute PE
Cancer-associated VTE: LMWH or apixaban preferred over warfarin
explanation.context: TAPSE measures longitudinal RV function; <17 mm indicates RV dysfunction. McConnell sign is RV free-wall akinesis with preserved apex, thought to reflect tethering by the LV. Together with troponin elevation (myocardial strain) and NT-proBNP (stretch), these define the intermediate-high tier that warrants escalation readiness without immediate lysis.

sources.label: PEITHO trial - Meyer et al., NEJM 2014
